entries.question: What is OpenScreenTime's design philosophy?
entries.answer: OpenScreenTime is built to be the opposite of an engagement-maximizing app. Its goal is to keep screen time something a family stays aware of, not something anyone ends up fixated on checking. So it shows a calm signal instead of running numbers, never scores failure (streaks only count up), interrupts with a pause rather than a wall, offers an off-ramp instead of a dead end, and keeps detailed reports with the parent - explained openly, as something to start a conversation.

entries.question: Is this meant for tracking my child secretly?
entries.answer: No. It's designed to support a conversation about healthy screen time, not to be sprung on someone unannounced. The kid app explains what it shows and why, and the weekly report says outright that it's meant to start a conversation with your child, not to track them silently. Talk to your child about it before installing.

entries.question: Can my child have a say in their limits?
entries.answer: Yes, on purpose. A child can use "Suggest a change" on their own phone (no passcode needed) to propose a different daily or per-app limit. It goes to a parent for approval and never changes anything by itself. Limits work better when they're negotiated than when they're only handed down.

entries.question: Does the app shame or punish going over a limit?
entries.answer: No. Streaks only ever count up from zero; there is no "broken streak" or "you missed a day" state anywhere. The daily tip is acknowledgment-only. A day over the limit is simply not counted, never flagged.

entries.question: Can my child get around the limits?
entries.answer: Some things are hard limits (a full-screen block, a parent lock) and some are deliberately deterrents. Android doesn't let an ordinary app truly prevent uninstalling it, so uninstall protection only adds a warning to ask a parent first. Bedtime text muting silences alerts but doesn't stop delivery. Anyone with physical access to a phone already has a baseline of trust, so the app is honest about what it can and can't enforce.

entries.question: What do the status icons mean?
entries.answer: A small icon in the top-left of the phone's status bar, next to the clock: a thumbs up ("Great job! You're on track."), an open hand ("Slow down"), or a stop sign ("You've reached your overall screen time limit"). Pull down from the top of the screen to see it as "Screen Time Status" with the same message. A stop sign also shows during a parent lock or bedtime, with a message saying screen time is paused. The kid app shows it, and the parent app shows the same icons once you turn on My screen time. Android always draws status-bar icons as flat white silhouettes; the color only shows in the pulled-down shade.

entries.question: Why can't my child see their exact numbers?
entries.answer: Deliberately. A running number invites checking, and compulsive checking is the behavior this app is trying not to feed. So the kid app only shows the calm icon, and the detailed report stays with the parent. A parent can choose to show unlock or notification counts on the kid's phone, but always alongside a note that watching counts can make phone use feel more compulsive.

entries.question: What is the streak?
entries.answer: A streak counts consecutive completed days under the current daily limit (and unlock goal, if one is set). It only ever counts up; a day with no synced data or a day over the limit simply means there's no streak to show, never a "broken" message.

entries.question: What is the friction pause?
entries.answer: The first time an app crosses half of its daily limit, a "Just a breath" screen appears and "Continue" is disabled for a few seconds. It's not a block - just a beat to notice the automatic reach for the app, and the choice to continue stays yours. It shows once per app per day.

entries.question: What is the block screen?
entries.answer: When a limit is reached, or it's bedtime, or a parent has paused screen time, a full-screen block appears. It suggests something else to do (except at bedtime, where winding down is the point) and has an OK button that takes you to the home screen. Swiping back doesn't dismiss it. During a limit or bedtime you can ask a parent for 5 or 15 more minutes.

entries.question: How do I ask for more time?
entries.answer: On the block screen, tap +5 min or +15 min. A parent sees the request in their app (or on the kid device under Parent controls) and can grant or decline it. A grant temporarily lets everything through - including bedtime - for that many minutes. It's never self-granted, and it can't override a parent lock.

entries.question: How do I suggest a different limit?
entries.answer: On the kid app's home screen, tap "Suggest a change", pick a new daily limit or a limit for a specific app, and send it. A parent reviews it and can approve or decline. Nothing changes until they approve, and no passcode is needed to send a suggestion.

entries.question: How do I pair my child's phone?
entries.answer: In the parent app tap +, name your child, and note the 6-digit code that appears. On the child's Android phone, open OpenScreenTime Kid and enter it. The code expires after 30 minutes. The child's phone signs in anonymously, so no email or personal info is collected from a child.

entries.question: Can two parents manage the same child?
entries.answer: Yes. Both parents sign in to the same parent account (email and password) on their own phones, Android or iPhone in any mix, and both see and control the same children. Nothing extra to set up.

entries.question: How do I set a daily screen time limit?
entries.answer: Open your child in the parent app and tap "Change daily limit". It's the total time the phone can be unlocked and in use per day, across all apps. The default is 120 minutes - a starting point, not a recommendation for every child (ask me about reasonable limits). You'll get a heads-up notification about 5 minutes before it's reached.

entries.question: How do I limit a specific app?
entries.answer: In your child's screen under "App usage today", tap Limit next to an app and set its daily minutes. Apps appear in that list once they've been used and synced. When the limit is reached that app is blocked; halfway there, the friction pause shows once.

entries.question: How do I set a bedtime?
entries.answer: Open your child and tap "Change bedtime". It's two steps, each with a clock and an AM or PM switch: first when bedtime starts (that evening or night, like 9:00 PM), then when it ends (the next morning, like 7:00 AM). A line underneath spells it out, for example "9:00 PM tonight to 7:00 AM tomorrow morning (10 hours)". During bedtime every app is blocked, independent of the daily limit. Apps you've marked "always allow" and numbers you've allowed for calls still get through. Bedtime is set per person: each child has their own, and your own "My screen time" has one too.

entries.question: How do I let certain apps always work?
entries.answer: In the app usage list, tick "Always allow" next to an app. It then stays usable through the daily limit, its own app limit, and bedtime - meant for things like a phone/calling app or maps. A parent lock still always wins.

entries.question: How do I block calls and texts at bedtime except from parents?
entries.answer: On the kid's phone, open Parent controls (passcode) and find "Bedtime calls". Add the numbers that may get through (like yours), then turn on incoming- and outgoing-call blocking (Android 10 or newer). During bedtime, calls from or to any other number are blocked. Texts can't be blocked, only quieted: with Notification access granted, the notification for a text from another number may be muted, but opening the messaging app still shows it, and it doesn't work with every messaging app. Calls from saved contacts may also ring through on some phones, so try it once with a test call.

entries.question: How do I pause screen time right now?
entries.answer: Tap "Lock now" on your child's card (or "End screen time now" on their screen). Every app on their phone is blocked immediately until you tap Resume. A lock is absolute - extra-time grants and always-allowed apps don't override it. You can also lift it from the locked phone itself: tap "Parent unlock" on the lock screen and enter the family passcode (set one from the parent app's home screen first).

entries.question: What are the family passcode and Parent controls?
entries.answer: Set a passcode in the parent app menu. It locks the parent app on launch, and it lets you open "Parent controls" on your child's own phone to change limits, bedtime, blocked websites, and more without needing your phone. The child's phone checks it locally against a stored hash, so it works offline. If you forget it, tap "Forgot passcode?" on the lock screen and confirm your account password to choose a new one. You can also let the parent app open with this phone's fingerprint or screen lock (Passcode settings) - only turn that on if a child can't unlock your phone. The kid's phone never accepts a fingerprint or screen lock, since the child's own would work.
entries.iosAnswer: Set a passcode in the parent app menu. It locks the parent app on launch, and it lets you open "Parent controls" on your child's own phone to change limits, bedtime, blocked websites, and more without needing your phone. The child's phone checks it locally against a stored hash, so it works offline.

entries.question: How do I reset my account password?
entries.answer: On the sign-in screen, enter your email and tap "Forgot password?". If there's an account for that email, you'll get a link to choose a new password - check your spam folder if it doesn't show up. This resets your account password only. The family passcode (the PIN under the menu's Passcode) is a separate thing.

entries.question: Can I see which websites my child visits?
entries.answer: Yes, if you turn it on: open your child, find Optional tracking, and switch on Track websites. It counts which SITES the phone looks up while a browser is open - site names only, never pages, searches, or time spent - and a bigger number means more activity, not a visit count. It needs the website filter turned on on that phone (Settings > Website filter), and it cannot see a browser that does its own private lookups: turn off Secure DNS in the browser and Private DNS in Android settings. Your child sees a note in their Settings saying it is on. It is off by default, and the same switch works for your own phone under My screen time.

entries.question: What is the weekly report?
entries.answer: Open your child and tap "View weekly report". It shows a rolling 4-week bar chart of total screen time, a weekly average, and a by-app trend for the top apps. It's capped at four weeks on purpose - enough to notice a trend, not an archive to pore over - and it never appears on the child's phone.
entries.iosAnswer: The weekly report isn't on the iPhone parent app yet - it's an Android parent app feature today, and porting it is one of the open items for the community. The iPhone app still shows each child's day-by-day numbers, limits, bedtime and tracking toggles.

entries.question: Why does it ask if I'm sure before opening the report?
entries.answer: After you've opened a report a few times in one day, it asks "Check in, not check up" before opening it again. It's the same friction-pause idea used on the kid side, turned on the parent: constant checking can become its own source of stress. You can still tap "Open anyway". The count is local to your phone and resets daily.
entries.iosAnswer: The weekly report, and so this pause, are Android parent app features today. The idea behind it applies anywhere, though: constant checking can become its own source of stress, so it's worth checking in on a rhythm rather than repeatedly.

entries.question: How do I turn on unlock or notification tracking?
entries.answer: Open your child (or your own "My screen time") and find "Optional tracking". Turn on Track unlocks and/or Track notification counts. Both are off by default. Track unlocks adds which app opens first after each unlock and puts unlocks in the weekly report and day-by-day digest (the plain daily unlock count is always kept, for the unlock goal). Nothing about notifications is collected until you turn that one on. Notification tracking counts only - never the content - and needs Notification access granted on that phone.
entries.iosAnswer: Open your child and find "Optional tracking". Turn on Track unlocks and/or Track notification counts. Both are off by default. The setting is saved for that child, and the kid's Android phone starts counting, but the iPhone parent app doesn't show the weekly report or day-by-day digest yet - that's an Android parent app feature today. Notification tracking counts only, never the content.

entries.question: How can I see which apps are opened right after unlocking?
entries.answer: Turn on Track unlocks. The weekly report then lists which apps were opened first after an unlock (within about 45 seconds; the home screen doesn't count). It's a good window into automatic reach-for-the-phone habits - a useful thing to discuss together rather than a score.

entries.question: Should I show counts on my child's phone?
entries.answer: It's optional and off by default. If you turn it on, today's count appears on their status screen with a note that watching counts can feed compulsive checking. Consider leaving it off unless your child has asked for it - a number that's always in view tends to invite checking.

entries.question: What is the calm notification list?
entries.answer: An optional list, kept only on the phone it's on, that groups the day's notifications by app so they can be read in one calm sitting. Turn it on from the kid's status screen or from the parent app's home screen; it needs Notification access.
entries.iosAnswer: The calm notification list is an Android feature, on both the kid and parent apps. The iPhone parent app doesn't have it yet.

entries.question: How do I block a website?
entries.answer: In your child's screen find "Blocked websites", type a domain such as tiktok.com and tap Block. It also blocks subdomains, in any browser, using a local filter on the child's phone (the "Website filter" permission on their status screen). Nothing is sent to a third-party server.

entries.question: Can I stop my child uninstalling the app?
entries.answer: Partly. In Parent controls on the child's phone, turn on "Uninstall protection". Removing the app then first shows a warning to ask a parent. Android doesn't let an ordinary app truly block uninstalling, so it's a deterrent, not a lock - someone who taps through the warning can still remove it.

entries.question: Can I track my own screen time too?
entries.answer: Yes, on Android. Tap the "My screen time" tile on the parent dashboard - the first time it asks to start tracking, and after that it opens your own screen time directly (permissions are under the "Permissions" button there). Your phone gets the same limits, bedtime, tracking, and report as a child's profile, and your child can see your calm status on their phone - the arrangement isn't one-directional. It isn't available on iPhone.

entries.question: Why does the kid app need so many permissions?
entries.answer: Accessibility service: to see which app is in front (it never reads screen content). Display over other apps: to show the block screen. Notifications: for the ongoing monitor notice and warnings. Battery optimization: so Android doesn't kill tracking. Website filter: for blocked sites. Optional extras (notification access, uninstall protection, call blocking) are only requested if you use those features.

entries.question: Tracking keeps stopping on a Samsung or Xiaomi phone
entries.answer: Some phone makers add battery rules beyond Android's standard one. After allowing the Battery optimization exemption, check the phone's own battery/app settings for options called "auto-start", "protected apps", or "sleeping apps" and allow OpenScreenTime. This is the known weak spot across brands.

entries.question: What data does the app collect?
entries.answer: It records time per app, unlock counts, and (only if a parent enables them) which app opens first after unlocking and notification counts - never notification content, messages, or what's on screen. It syncs to the Firebase project your family set up, not to any central server. The optional notification list stays on the child's phone. Crash reports contain stack traces and device model only.

entries.question: Does it work on iPhone?
entries.answer: The iPhone app is for parents only. There is no OpenScreenTime Kid for iPhone yet, because Apple hasn't granted the Family Controls entitlement a kid-side app needs, so a child has to be paired using an Android phone. An iPhone parent can fully manage that Android child. If your child uses an iPhone, Apple's own Screen Time (in Settings) is the closest built-in option.

entries.question: What is grayscale mode and should I use it?
entries.answer: Grayscale makes apps less visually compelling to check. It's recommended, not forced, and the app can't switch it on for you - open Accessibility settings and look for "Color correction" or "Color and motion"; the exact wording varies by phone.

entries.question: Is OpenScreenTime free? Where does my data live?
entries.answer: It's free and open source (MIT) with no ads or subscriptions. There's no central server: each family points the apps at their own free Firebase project, so the data lives in an account you control.

entries.question: How do I send feedback or report a bug?
entries.answer: In the parent app's menu (the three dots), choose Feedback and write your note - it goes straight to the maintainers without revealing anyone's address. You can also open an issue on the project's GitHub page.

entries.question: How much screen time is reasonable?
entries.answer: There isn't one number that fits every child. The strongest numeric guidance is for young children: the WHO advises no screen time for under-2s and no more than 1 hour a day (less is better) for ages 2 to 4. For ages 5 to 17 the Canadian guidelines suggest no more than 2 hours a day of recreational screen time, while the American Academy of Pediatrics and UK Chief Medical Officers say the evidence doesn't support one fixed limit and point to quality, sleep, and activity instead. Tell me your child's age for the specifics. This is general public guidance, not medical advice.

entries.question: How much screen time for a baby or toddler under 2?
entries.answer: The WHO says screen time is not recommended for infants under 1, and sedentary screen time (TV, videos, games) is not recommended for 1-year-olds. The AAP notes infants under 18 months learn best from real-world interactions, and heavy solo screen use can affect developing language and social skills. Reading, play, and time with a caregiver are the better use of that time. General guidance, not medical advice.

sources.title: AAP: helping kids thrive in a digital world

entries.question: How much screen time for a 2, 3 or 4 year old?
entries.answer: The WHO advises no more than 1 hour a day of sedentary screen time for ages 2 to 4, and adds that less is better. It also emphasizes replacing screen time with active play, reading and storytelling with a caregiver, and good sleep (10 to 13 hours a day for ages 3 to 4, 11 to 14 for age 2, including naps). General guidance, not medical advice.

entries.question: How much screen time for a school-age child or teen?
entries.answer: The Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines suggest no more than 2 hours a day of recreational screen time for ages 5 to 17, alongside at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity and 9 to 11 hours of sleep (ages 5 to 13) or 8 to 10 hours (ages 14 to 17). The AAP and UK Chief Medical Officers say the evidence doesn't support one fixed limit for everyone, and recommend focusing on what screens crowd out. Note: 2 hours refers to recreational use - schoolwork isn't counted, but this app counts all screen time. General guidance, not medical advice.

entries.question: What does the American Academy of Pediatrics say about screen time?
entries.answer: The AAP says there isn't enough evidence to support a single screen-time limit that applies to all children and teens. It recommends looking at quality as well as quantity - content, co-viewing, calm, what media crowds out, and communication - and building a Family Media Plan together. Its 2026 guidance stresses moving beyond simple limits toward quality, context, and conversation, with screen-free zones (bedrooms, mealtimes) and no screens for an hour before bed.

sources.title: AAP: helping kids thrive in a digital world

entries.question: Is there evidence that screen time harms mental health?
entries.answer: The UK Chief Medical Officers' review found an association between screen time and mental health problems in children and young people, but the evidence wasn't clear enough to show that screens cause them, and was insufficient to set an evidence-based time limit. That's why much current guidance focuses on sleep, activity, content, and how a child feels and behaves rather than a single number.

entries.question: How should screens fit around sleep?
entries.answer: The AAP recommends screen-free zones - bedrooms and mealtimes are good places to start - and no screens for an hour before bed. For sleep amounts, the Canadian guidelines suggest 9 to 11 hours a night for ages 5 to 13 and 8 to 10 hours for ages 14 to 17; the WHO gives 10 to 13 hours for ages 3 to 4. A bedtime window in this app (and keeping the phone out of the bedroom) supports that. General guidance, not medical advice.

sources.title: AAP: helping kids thrive in a digital world

entries.question: How much screen time should I set for myself?
entries.answer: No major health body publishes a daily screen-time number for adults, so it's yours to set. A practical way to choose: decide what you want more of (sleep, movement, time with family, focus), see your real numbers for a week using self-tracking, then set a limit slightly below your current use and adjust. Modeling healthy habits is one of the things the AAP recommends for parents, and children notice. This is a practical suggestion, not medical advice.

entries.question: How do I decide on a limit for my child?
entries.answer: A practical approach, in the spirit of the AAP's Family Media Plan: first protect the non-negotiables - sleep, physical activity, homework, meals, and family time. Then see what's left and set a starting daily limit together with your child. Use the weekly report to notice patterns, and revisit it every few weeks. Age matters: ask me about your child's age for what public guidance says. A limit your child helped set is more likely to stick than one imposed on them.

entries.question: Does the type of screen time matter, not just the amount?
entries.answer: Yes. The AAP recommends considering the quality of interactions with digital media, not just the amount of time, and reports that rules based on balance, content, co-viewing, and communication are linked to better well-being than rules based only on time. Creating, learning, or connecting with people is different from endless scrolling. Use per-app limits and always-allowed apps to reflect that.

entries.question: Why is the default limit 120 minutes?
entries.answer: It's simply a starting value, in the same range as the Canadian 2-hours-a-day recreational figure for ages 5 to 17 - not a recommendation for every child. It's too high for a preschooler under WHO guidance and may not suit your family. Also note this app counts all unlocked screen time, including schoolwork, while that guideline refers to recreational use. Adjust it to your child's age and your household.
